title: Overview
text: Overview Why simulation? It lets us try an action in a modeled world, calculate what happens, and repeat the experiment with different conditions. This free online book follows one familiar task: opening a drawer. We begin with how AI models understand instructions, then build the 3D object and describe how it moves. Simple explanations, illustrations, and moving examples connect these ideas. Language, vision, and robot actions — understanding a request, reading a picture, and choosing a movement. 3D representations, reconstruction, and generation — what is stored, how it becomes an image, and how methods create it. Articulated objects — parts, joints, and URDF files. Simulation — preparing a physical model, testing forces, and adding robot interaction.

title: 1. Language, vision, and robot actions
text: 1. Language, vision, and robot actions Explaining how to open a drawer, finding its handle in a picture, and commanding a robot to pull it require different abilities. This chapter uses the same cabinet to introduce three kinds of model: a large language model (LLM) , a vision-language model (VLM) , and a vision-language-action model (VLA) . We will compare what information each receives and what it produces. We will also distinguish understanding a picture from generating one, and see how an assistant can call another model to help with either task. One cabinet, three abilities Explain the task. Locate the handle. Choose an action. The inputs and outputs of the three cabinet examples Model Example input Example output LLM “How do I open a drawer?” Written instructions. VLM Cabinet image + “Where is the handle?” An answer based on the image. VLA Robot camera image + “Open the drawer.” Movement and gripper commands.

title: LLM: work with language
text: 1.1 LLM: work with language A large language model (LLM) learns patterns in language and can generate answers, explanations, or instructions. For the drawer task, we can describe the problem in words and ask it to suggest steps. Input: “How do you open a drawer?” Possible text output: “Hold the handle and pull outward.” This answer explains the task. With only that written request, the model has no picture showing where this cabinet’s handle is. Here, generating an answer means producing text . The term LLM describes language capability. Some models also accept images or other kinds of input; the next example uses that visual capability.

title: VLM: connect images and words
text: 1.2 VLM: connect images and words A vision-language model (VLM) combines visual information with language. Given the cabinet image and a question, it can connect the words “drawer handle” to a particular part of the picture. LLaVA is one example: its image-processing component passes visual information to a language model. A chat example: add a cabinet picture A model that supports both text and images can handle either message below. The question stays the same; the information we provide changes. Words alone “Where is this cabinet’s drawer handle?” No picture or description identifies this cabinet. A possible reply: “Please send a picture or describe the cabinet.” Picture + words “Where is this cabinet’s drawer handle?” The image shows which part is the drawer. A possible reply: “On the blue drawer at the top.” These are illustrative replies. With the picture, the answer can refer to this cabinet , using visual information as well as words. One model can understand words and pictures LLM emphasizes language ability; VLM emphasizes combining vision and language. The labels can overlap. A model that handles more than one kind of information, such as text and images, is called multimodal . GPT-4o , for example, was trained to process text and images within one model. When it receives the cabinet picture, it can use its own visual capability to answer. Uploading a picture therefore does not, by itself, mean that the application has switched models. Reading a picture and generating one Understand the cabinet picture Input: the existing picture + “Where is the drawer handle?” Output: “On the blue drawer at the top.” The task is to interpret what the supplied picture shows. Create a cabinet picture Input: “Draw a blue cabinet with a gold door.” Output: a new image of a cabinet. Editing is another image-generation task: supply a picture and ask to change the door’s color. Both tasks can appear in the same chat application. Their requested outputs are different: an answer about an image, or an image itself. OpenAI’s image guide describes both uses. How can an assistant call another model? A chat application can connect its main model to other models through tools . The assistant requests a tool, and the application sends the required inputs to it and returns the result. This lets the assistant delegate a task. Call a VLM to read the picture Assistant requests help Ask a visual tool to locate the drawer handle. VLM examines the image The application supplies the cabinet picture and question. The VLM returns a description of the handle’s location. Assistant uses the result Answer: “On the blue drawer at the top.” This is an alternative to the main model reading the image itself. HuggingGPT is a research example of an LLM selecting other models and using their results to compose a response. Call an image model to draw a picture Assistant requests an image Send “Draw a blue cabinet with a gold door” to an image-generation tool. Image model creates it The model generates an image from the description. Application displays it The new cabinet picture appears in the conversation. OpenAI’s image-generation tool supports this arrangement: a main model can call a separate GPT Image model to generate or edit an image. Reading and drawing name the tasks. Calling a tool describes how the work is assigned. A model with its own vision capability can still call another model to create pictures.

title: VLA: produce robot actions
text: 1.3 VLA: produce robot actions A vision-language-action model (VLA) uses visual information and an instruction to produce robot actions. Depending on the model, it may also use information about the robot’s current position. For the cabinet task, the input is the robot’s camera image and “Open the drawer.” The output can be numbers telling its gripper —the robot’s grasping hand—where to move and whether to open or close. A robot controller turns those commands into signals for the robot’s motors. The next camera image shows what actually happened. Opening a drawer, step by step In this example, the gripper is already holding the handle. The diagram illustrates one possible action, not a recorded prediction from a trained model. 1 Camera image + instruction Drawer: 0 cm open Gripper: holding the handle Instruction “Open the drawer.” The image shows the current situation. The words give the task. 2 Process the image and instruction This example follows the broad structure of OpenVLA . These components work together within the VLA. Image encoder + adapter Turn the image into numerical features the main model can use. Vision-language backbone Combine those features with the instruction “Open the drawer.” Action output Produce action values. Here, a possible result is an outward movement with the gripper kept closed. 3 A possible command Move outward +0.10 m Gripper Keep closed In words: “Move the gripper 10 cm outward while holding the handle.” These are two readable fields for this one-direction example. A real robot’s command format can include more movement values. 4 Controller → movement → new image The controller tries to execute the command. If the drawer slides freely and the grip holds, the drawer can follow the gripper outward. Possible result: 10 cm open If the drawer is locked, it stays at 0 cm instead. The next camera image shows the actual result, so the next prediction can use that new information. ↺ The new camera image goes back to step 1. The model can then choose another action. What does “predict an action” mean? A VLA is trained using examples that pair observations and instructions with robot actions. It learns patterns in those examples. When given a new image and instruction, it uses what it learned to produce the next action values. For the same instruction, “Open the drawer,” different views can call for different commands: What the image shows Example next command The open gripper is positioned around the handle. Move 0 cm ; close the gripper to grasp it. The gripper is already holding the handle. Move 10 cm outward ; keep closed . These are illustrative commands. Here, “predict” means propose the next action . The structure is simplified from OpenVLA , whose predicted outputs are decoded into numerical robot commands. Other VLAs can organize their action outputs differently. What happens after the robot tries to pull? The VLA proposes a movement; the controller tries to carry it out. A freely sliding drawer may follow the gripper, while a locked drawer stays shut. The next observation helps the model choose what to do next. This interaction can happen with a real cabinet or in a simulation. In simulation, a physics engine calculates the movement, and a renderer produces the next camera image. Robot interaction in Chapter 4 explains how the model, controller, and simulator work together.

title: 2.1 How do we represent a 3D cabinet?
text: 2.1 How do we represent a 3D cabinet? General introduction A photograph stores an image from one viewpoint. A 3D representation stores information about the cabinet in space, so software can inspect it or calculate views from other positions. Sections 2.1 – 2.3 introduce general concepts. Sections 2.4 – 2.7 show how specific tools and methods use them.

title: What is stored?
text: 2.1.1 What is stored? A representation is a way of describing an object with data. For the same cabinet, we might save individual 3D points, connected surface patches, soft colored blobs, or a function that answers questions about locations in space. All four can describe the cabinet in 3D, but they store different information. Start with what each contains; the next sections explain how software uses it to draw a picture. The drawings below show these different data layouts using one teaching cabinet: a teal body, a blue drawer, and a gold door. Point cloud Store: a list of 3D positions, sometimes with colors. Points can outline the drawer and handle. The list does not specify which points form a continuous surface. Mesh Store: 3D corner positions, called vertices, and surface patches, called faces, connecting them. The faces describe the cabinet’s surfaces. A face can have three sides (a triangle) or four (a quad). 3D Gaussians Store: each blob’s position, size, orientation, opacity, and appearance. Each blob is a soft shape in 3D. Its opacity controls how strongly its color contributes and hides what is behind it. Many blue blobs can form the drawer’s image. Radiance field Describe: the color seen from a direction and the density at locations in 3D. Density controls how strongly a small region blocks the view. Near the drawer front, the answers may be blue and strongly blocking; in the air, almost no blocking. NeRF uses a neural network to supply these answers. The dots mark example queries, not a stored point cloud. A Gaussian is a soft 3D shape, not just a colored point. A radiance field describes visibility and appearance; its density does not specify the cabinet’s physical mass. We will see how these representations produce pictures in Section 2.3 . Further reading: point clouds , mesh structure , 3D Gaussians , and NeRF’s radiance field .

title: Representation, method, and renderer
text: 2.1.2 Representation, method, and renderer Making a 3D cabinet involves three different roles: a method creates the data, a representation specifies what is kept, and a renderer turns it into a picture. Representation What information do we keep? For example, the cabinet’s vertices and faces, or a set of 3D Gaussians. Reconstruction or generation method How do we obtain that information? Reconstruction tries to recover the cabinet seen in photographs. A generator can propose a cabinet using patterns learned from many examples, including guesses about unseen parts. Renderer How do we make a picture from it? Software uses the representation and a camera to calculate a 2D image. A method’s supported outputs depend on its design. Some methods produce surface geometry; some produce Gaussians; others support several representations. We first learn what those outputs contain, then follow how methods create them. For example: a method creates the cabinet as a mesh → we save its surface data → a mesh renderer draws a front view. The saved 3D data can also be used to draw a side view.

title: 2.2 Meshes: surfaces and useful detail
text: 2.2 Meshes: surfaces and useful detail General introduction

title: Meshes: surfaces and useful detail
text: A mesh describes surface shape using connected patches . For a drawer, these can describe the outside, the inner walls, and the bottom. The empty space inside the drawer stays empty: a surface mesh does not mean the whole object is filled with material. A point cloud records sampled positions in 3D. A mesh also records how positions connect to form surfaces. The positions are called vertices, their connections are edges, and the surface patches are faces. Moving the positions changes the shape; changing their connections changes how the surface is assembled. Point cloud Useful for recording measurements. Gaps may mean an area was never observed, rather than a real hole. Triangle mesh Three-sided surface patches. Each triangle is flat, which makes its shape straightforward to calculate and draw. Quad mesh Four-sided surface patches. Regular rows can be convenient for editing. Software can divide them into triangles to draw the surface. Triangle and quad meshes on the same cabinet Both are surface meshes. In a quad mesh , each face has four sides. In a triangle mesh , each face has three. The cabinet below uses the same corner positions and camera in both views; only the face connections change. Quad faces Regular rows make it convenient to select and reshape a strip of the surface. Triangle faces Each four-sided patch here is divided into two triangles. The cabinet’s shape stays the same. Triangles are always flat, so they are convenient for rendering. A quad can be split into triangles for this purpose. Editing software can let us work with quads while using triangles to draw the result. Blender’s triangulation tool. Face type alone does not determine the shape’s accuracy. The curved-handle examples below show why the positions of the vertices matter too. Building a mesh from measured points is called surface reconstruction . It must infer which samples belong together; blindly filling every gap could seal the opening around a drawer. Open3D’s examples show several ways to estimate these surfaces. Why can a mesh look angular? A round bar has a curved surface. A mesh builds that surface from flat pieces . Imagine joining flat strips around the bar: a few wide strips make obvious corners; many narrow strips follow the curve more closely. 6 faces around the side Each face is wide. Look at the top edge: the bar has clear corners. 32 faces around the side Each face is narrower. The top edge comes much closer to a circle. Both models approximate the same round bar and use the same camera view. The lines show where the mesh faces meet. This is why the number of faces can matter: more, smaller faces can represent a curve more closely , when their corners are placed along that curve. A flat cabinet panel needs much less detail because its surface is already flat. More faces also mean more data to store and process. We choose enough to describe the shape we need; the highest face count is not automatically the best choice. The same idea on a cabinet These two cabinets have the same flat panels. Only the round handles change: each bar has 6 sides on the left and 32 sides on the right . The enlarged drawer handle makes the difference easier to see. 228 triangular faces 84 on the flat panels + 144 on the handles. The round handles have visible corners. 852 triangular faces The same 84 panel faces + 768 handle faces. The handles follow the round shape more closely. The camera and colors are the same in both pictures. The lines mark the edges of the triangular faces. The extra faces improve the curved handles; the flat cabinet panels stay unchanged. For software used to inspect and edit these surfaces, see the 3D software guide .

title: 2.3 How a 3D model produces a 2D image
text: 2.3 How a 3D model produces a 2D image General introduction

title: Render mesh surfaces
text: 2.3.1 Render mesh surfaces Sections 2.1 and 2.2 described the stored data. Rendering starts with that data already available and asks what a camera would see. A mesh supplies the surfaces of objects in a scene . A scene also specifies where those objects are placed, where the camera looks, and how surfaces are colored and lit. The renderer uses that information to calculate an image. A texture is often an image placed on a surface, like a printed pattern. A material controls how the surface responds to light—for example, whether a handle looks like dull plastic or shiny metal. Which tool makes these pictures? A renderer is the software that calculates the picture. We give it a 3D scene and a virtual camera: where the camera is, which way it looks, and how wide its view is. The software calculates the pixels and saves the result as an image. Think of photographing a cabinet from the left, front, and right. In rendering, we place a virtual camera at those three positions. We keep the same 3D cabinet and calculate a new picture from each position. What we have Example tool What we do A mesh Blender , using a renderer such as Eevee or Cycles. Load the model, set its appearance, place lights and a camera, then render and save an image. 3D Gaussians A Gaussian renderer, such as gsplat . Load the blobs and choose a camera. The renderer projects the blobs and blends their colors into the image. A trained NeRF A NeRF volume renderer, such as the one in the original NeRF implementation . Load the trained network and choose a camera. Query color and density along camera rays, then combine the answers into pixels. For this book’s Gaussian cabinet videos, we wrote a small renderer in Python. It calculates the projected marks and their color mixtures. The left, front, and right pictures all come from the same cabinet data. Rendering many frames while moving the camera, then joining those frames into a video, gives the moving-camera example below . A screenshot can record a picture already displayed by a viewer. Here, the renderer saves its calculated images directly. Stored surfaces The mesh gives the cabinet its shape and depth. One camera view The surfaces become colored areas in an image. The construction edges need not be visible. One common mesh-rendering process is rasterization : Project the triangles. Use the camera’s position, viewing direction, and lens to map their 3D corners to 2D image positions. With a perspective camera, a farther object generally appears smaller. Find what each pixel sees. Work out which projected triangles cover it. For opaque surfaces, keep the nearest visible surface; a closed door hides what is behind it. Calculate the color. Use the visible surface’s material, texture, direction, and lighting. Repeat across the image. Imagine walking around a real cabinet: the cabinet stays still, but you see a different side. A virtual camera works similarly. Keep the 3D cabinet in place, move the camera from the front to the side, and render again. The new image shows the surfaces visible from the side. We do not need to rebuild the mesh for that camera movement. This is what the mesh contributes: the cabinet’s surfaces in 3D . The camera chooses the view, and the renderer calculates the picture. More on rendering . Renderers can also make pictures from other representations. For 3D Gaussians , the renderer blends the blobs’ projected colors. For a NeRF radiance field , it asks a network about locations along each line of sight. The examples below use these two ways to calculate a picture.

title: Rendering Gaussians: projection, videos, and opacity
text: 2.3.2 Gaussian rendering: project and blend A 3D Gaussian representation stores many soft 3D blobs. Each has a position, size, orientation, opacity, and appearance. Imagine one small blue patch on the drawer front. A blob can be wide across that patch but thin from front to back . In the rendered picture, its blue color is strongest at the center and gradually fades toward the edges, like a soft spray-painted spot. Many overlapping spots can form the picture of the whole drawer. How do the 3D blobs become an image? A Gaussian renderer projects each 3D blob onto the flat image as a soft oval mark. Where marks overlap, it combines their colors, taking account of which blob is nearer the camera. Placing and blending these projected marks is called splatting . Original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) project . Watch the 3D setup become a 2D view The image plane is a flat rectangle where we draw the camera’s picture. In this diagram it sits in front of the camera. Seen from its edge, that rectangle looks like a line; the image still has width and height. Open the projection video . 0:00 · The setup 0:06 · Project the blobs 0:16 · Look from the edge 0:26 · Face the image 0:36 · Move the camera First, we rotate our view of the diagram to see the image plane from the side and front. In the last part, the camera itself moves while the two 3D blobs stay in place. The picture on the right shows exactly what that camera renders. The outlined shapes help us see the blobs in 3D. Their rendered marks have soft edges because a Gaussian fades outward. Download the video In the last part, watch the gold mark move behind the blue one, then separate again. The 3D blobs have not moved: the camera now sees them along different lines of sight. Their marks are calculated again for each new camera position. This is how the same 3D scene can produce different 2D pictures. For implementation details, see how gsplat uses the camera and Gaussian shapes to calculate these images . Now try a whole cabinet The same idea works with many blobs. Here, blue blobs form the drawer, gold blobs form the door, and teal blobs form the cabinet body. First we enlarge one drawer blob; then we follow the cabinet’s colors onto the image plane and move the camera. Open the cabinet video . 0:00 · The cabinet 0:10 · One blob, enlarged 0:24 · Project onto the image 0:38 · Move the camera 0:56 · Compare three views The outlined shapes make the individual blobs visible. The camera picture blends their soft marks together. The cabinet stays still throughout; only the camera moves. This is a deliberately simple teaching model we built, not a reconstruction trained from photographs. Download the cabinet video What does changing opacity actually change? Several blobs can cover the same spot in the camera’s picture. We need one final color at that spot. Opacity decides how strongly the front blob contributes and how much of the color behind it can still show through. In the cabinet video, overlapping blue marks combine to form the drawer’s picture. Opacity is part of that blending step. It does not add paint or a texture to a mesh. Try a blue mark in front of a gold mark. Move the slider and watch how much gold remains visible. The gold stays at 80% opacity; only the blue changes. Two soft projected ellipses overlap at a marked pixel, with the blue contribution in front of the gold One pixel The marked pixel receives color from both overlapping blobs. Blue opacity at the marked pixel 25% Try 25% Try 85% The resulting pixel 25% blue + 60% gold + 15% white background. Blue uses 25% of the pixel’s weight. Gold gets 80% of the remaining 75%: 60%. The background gets the last 15%. Low blue opacity: more gold shows through. High blue opacity: the picture becomes mostly blue at the marked spot. Neither blob has moved; we have changed how their colors combine. The calculation follows one pixel. Across the whole picture, each mark fades toward its edges, and many marks overlap to make the cabinet’s surfaces look continuous. The 3DGS paper gives the projection and blending equations. Change opacity on the whole cabinet Now change the opacity of every blob in the cabinet . The camera, colors, positions, and sizes stay the same. Compare your setting on the right with the fixed picture on the left. 95% per blob · reference 5% per blob · your setting Opacity of each cabinet blob 5% Try 5% Try 25% Try 95% At 5%, the faint marks let more of the rear surfaces and white background show through. Many blobs overlap. Their colors build up, so 25% per blob does not mean that the whole cabinet is only 25% opaque. At 0%, none of the blobs contributes color and only the white background remains.

title: Rendering a radiance field
text: 2.3.3 Rendering a radiance field For a radiance field, begin with one image pixel. The camera defines a line of sight through that pixel into the scene. The renderer samples locations along that line and asks the field for color and density there. Along a line toward the drawer, empty air contributes little. Locations near the blue front panel contribute blue and reduce the contribution from behind. Combining the answers produces the pixel’s color. Repeating this across the image produces a view of the cabinet. Sample locations along one ray contribute to one image pixel. Section 2.6 follows these queries and their answers in detail. In NeRF, a trained network supplies those answers. Its volume renderer combines them into pixels. Section 2.6.5 continues this cabinet example.

title: Use rendering to check a 3D estimate
text: 2.3.4 Use rendering to check a 3D estimate So far, we have started with 3D data and made an image. Reconstruction starts from photographs and estimates the 3D information that could explain them. Rendering gives us a way to check that estimate. Estimate 3D Propose a cabinet representation from its photographs. Render and compare Draw that representation from the photograph’s camera and compare the two images. If the rendered handle appears in the wrong place, the 3D estimate may need to change. The original 3DGS and NeRF methods repeat this comparison across several camera views. Adjusting a representation to match the observed images is called fitting . The photographs are the evidence; the 3D representation is what we adjust. Rendering is the check that connects them: it lets us compare a picture made from the estimate with an actual input picture.

title: 2.4 Recover cameras and geometry from photographs
text: 2.4 Recover cameras and geometry from photographs Tools and models · COLMAP software and the VGGT model To reconstruct the cabinet, collect overlapping views of it. We need to relate those flat photographs to camera viewpoints and locations in 3D space.

title: What information do we need?
text: 2.4.1 What information do we need? Keep the cabinet, door, and drawer still while photographing from different positions. The images are the observations we want the reconstruction to explain. Camera parameters Where was the camera, which way did it point, and what were its lens settings for each image? These determine the line of sight for each pixel. Geometry estimates Where might the cabinet’s surfaces be in 3D? Depth estimates and 3D points provide information about their locations. Each input photograph must be associated with its own camera information. COLMAP and VGGT offer two ways to estimate this information from photographs. COLMAP matches details across views; VGGT uses patterns learned during prior training. When camera positions and settings are already known, we can supply those values directly.

title: COLMAP: match details across views
text: 2.4.2 COLMAP: match details across views COLMAP is software that estimates cameras and 3D points by finding the same details in different photographs. The cabinet drawings below illustrate this process. Follow the marked drawer corner: View 1 View 2 View 3 A marks the same cabinet corner in all three views. Software matches recognizable details across photos. From many such matches, it estimates where the cameras were and where the details sit in 3D. Locate one point. Each view gives a line of sight toward A. Combining views estimates its depth. Repeat for many details. The result is sparse: scattered points, with gaps between them. This camera-and-point estimation is called Structure from Motion (SfM) . COLMAP is one tool for it. A plain, featureless panel can provide few reliable matches; we do not yet have a complete cabinet surface. The sparse reconstruction provides camera parameters and scattered 3D points . Keep the input photographs too: later stages will compare rendered images with them. This example stops at COLMAP’s sparse stage; COLMAP also has tools for denser reconstruction.

title: VGGT: predict cameras and geometry
text: 2.4.3 VGGT: predict cameras and geometry VGGT (Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer) is a model that estimates camera parameters and geometry from images. It is pretrained : it has already learned from many scenes before receiving these cabinet photographs. For a new cabinet, it uses that prior learning to predict where the cameras and surfaces are. VGGT project. Input Cabinet images → VGGT A pretrained geometry model → Outputs Cameras + depth / 3D points Output Meaning for the cabinet Camera parameters An estimated viewpoint and lens for each photograph. Depth map A grid aligned with the image, giving an estimated depth for each pixel. It tells us how far into the scene the visible surface lies. Point map Image locations are associated with predicted positions in 3D. For example, a drawer corner gets a 3D location. For example, VGGT can estimate a 3D position for the drawer corner and a camera viewpoint for each image. Its export tool can save those cameras and points in COLMAP’s file format. Here, “COLMAP format” means an arrangement of files that other software can read; the estimates can still come from VGGT. To obtain a Gaussian scene, continue with a Gaussian training method. The official VGGT integration passes the images, estimated cameras, and points to gsplat, a Gaussian rendering and training library. Training then adjusts the Gaussians to match the cabinet photographs.

title: Where do these outputs go next?
text: 2.4.4 Where do these outputs go next? Choose a reconstruction method after preparing the inputs. 3DGS and NeRF are two alternatives. Both keep the cabinet photographs as target images: render from the estimated cameras, compare with the photos, and improve the 3D representation. Continue with 3DGS Use estimated 3D points as starting locations for Gaussians. Use each camera to render the current Gaussians from its photograph’s viewpoint. Compare with that photograph and adjust the Gaussians. Saved result: the fitted Gaussian parameters. Follow the cabinet in Section 2.5 Continue with NeRF Use each camera to construct rays through image pixels. Sample positions along those rays and query a network for color and density. Render pixels, compare with the photographs, and adjust the network. Saved result: a trained network that describes the cabinet. Follow the cabinet in Section 2.6 The 3D points play different roles. In the 3DGS route, estimated surface points provide starting locations for blobs. In the original NeRF route, the renderer chooses query locations along camera rays, including in empty space. Those locations need not coincide with COLMAP’s or VGGT’s estimated surface points. Each query position and viewing direction is sent to the NeRF network. The worked examples below use COLMAP-style camera preparation. The VGGT export offers another way to supply camera and point estimates; the later rendering and fitting stages still need to be carried out. Further details: original 3DGS inputs and original NeRF camera preparation .

title: 2.5 Reconstruct a cabinet with 3DGS
text: 2.5 Reconstruct a cabinet with 3DGS Specific method · 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) First, train: use multiple views of the cabinet and their camera information to adjust the 3D Gaussians. Repeatedly render images, compare with the photographs, and update the Gaussians. Then, render: use the saved Gaussians and a new virtual camera position and settings to produce another view of the same cabinet. No photograph from that new angle is needed.

title: Inputs and output of Gaussian reconstruction
text: Start with the prepared inputs The COLMAP example in Section 2.4.2 estimates camera viewpoints and sparse 3D points. These points provide initial blob locations. The VGGT export in Section 2.4.3 is another supported source of cameras and starting points for a Gaussian training pipeline. Each initial Gaussian also needs size, orientation, opacity, and appearance. Fitting adjusts these values using the photographs. The result is a set of Gaussian parameters we can save and render from another camera. Section 2.3.2 showed how to project and blend a given set of Gaussians. Here we use that same rendering operation repeatedly to find better Gaussians.

title: Fit the cabinet Gaussians to photographs
text: Fit the cabinet to its photographs This is a teaching diagram. Rendered cabinet views stand in for photographs; the stages below illustrate the process, rather than showing a recorded training run. 1. Put an initial blob at each 3D point Initial 3D blobs Points now have size, color, and opacity. Their rendered 2D image The drawer and handle look blurry. Reference view The image we want to match. Compare from the same camera position. Otherwise, a difference could simply come from looking at the cabinet from a different angle. 2. Use the image differences to update the blobs Render 3D blobs → 2D image → Compare Rendered image ↔ photo → Update Change the 3D blobs ↶ Render again, compare again, update again. The comparison gives an error: how different are the images? The fitting process uses that error to adjust the blobs. For example, several smaller blobs can describe the handle more precisely than one large, blurry blob. Adjust Change position, size, orientation, color, or opacity. Add detail Clone a blob, or split a large one into smaller ones. Remove Discard blobs with very low opacity. These changes happen in 3D , so they affect several camera views. The original 3DGS method alternates parameter updates with adding and removing blobs. 3. Keep checking the other views, too A closer match Many overlapping blobs form a clearer cabinet image. A new camera view Render the same 3D blobs from another position. Fitting repeats across the photographs so that one set of 3D blobs explains many views . We save those blobs and can then render new views. This is the purpose of the 3DGS representation ; it does not automatically add a drawer joint or the cabinet’s mass.

title: 2.6 NeRF: from cabinet photos to new views
text: 2.6 NeRF: from cabinet photos to new views Specific method · Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) First, train: use multiple views of the cabinet and their camera information to train a network representing the cabinet in 3D. Repeatedly render images, compare with the photographs, and update the network. Then, render: use the saved network and a new virtual camera position and settings to produce another view of the same cabinet. No photograph from that new angle is needed.

title: NeRF: photograph one cabinet
text: 2.6.1 Photograph the cabinet Take overlapping photographs from several positions. Keep the cabinet, drawer, and door still. Each photograph shows the same scene from a different viewpoint. Photo 1 · from the left Photo 2 · from the front Photo 3 · from the right The original NeRF is trained separately for each scene. Photographs of this cabinet provide the training images: the network learns a description of this particular cabinet from those views. The three views illustrate the image collection step. Reconstruction may use many more photographs to cover the scene.

title: Prepare NeRF inputs: images and camera parameters
text: 2.6.2 Prepare images and camera parameters The NeRF training pipeline takes the scene’s images and each image’s camera position, orientation, and lens parameters as input. Position specifies where the camera was; orientation specifies which way it pointed. Lens parameters, such as focal length, determine how the scene projects onto the image. Each cabinet image is associated with the camera position and orientation used to capture that view. Use the camera estimates from Section 2.4 Section 2.4.2 explains how COLMAP estimates cameras from the cabinet photographs. Section 2.4.3 introduces VGGT’s camera and geometry predictions. Either route must supply camera data in the form expected by the chosen NeRF implementation. In the workflow illustrated here, COLMAP supplies the camera estimates. Keep each photograph paired with its camera position, orientation, and lens parameters. The original NeRF code describes this preparation. Prepared inputs Cabinet photos + camera parameters → NeRF renderer Rays + sampled 3D positions → NeRF network Color + density per sample NeRF starts from the photos and cameras, not from the fitted Gaussian scene in Section 2.5. The 3DGS and NeRF routes branch after input preparation. In NeRF, the renderer calculates the sample positions sent to the network. NeRF training sequence Estimate the cameras. COLMAP processes the cabinet photographs and estimates the camera parameters associated with each image. Calculate rays and sample positions. NeRF’s renderer uses the camera parameters to construct a ray through a selected pixel, then samples 3D positions along that ray. Query the neural network. Each sample position and its viewing direction enter the network, which predicts a color and density. Render and compare. The renderer combines those predictions into a pixel color and compares it with the corresponding pixel in the cabinet photograph. Update the network. The training algorithm adjusts the network’s numerical settings, called weights, to reduce the color error. Steps 2–5 repeat across pixels and camera views. COLMAP supplies camera estimates during data preparation. The repeated training loop updates the NeRF network . The photographs provide target colors; the renderer calculates the positions and directions sent to the network. Section 2.6.4 illustrates the ray and sample positions for one cabinet pixel.

title: What Neural Radiance Field means and what the network learns
text: 2.6.3 Create a network that can answer questions about space NeRF stands for Neural Radiance Field . The name describes a learned rule for answering two questions at a place in 3D: Color The color a location contributes when viewed from a particular direction. At the blue drawer front, the expected contribution is blue. Density How strongly does a small interval here contribute and block what is behind it? Air should contribute almost nothing; the blue panel should strongly affect the picture. Neural refers to the learned program. Radiance refers to the light or color seen from a direction. Field means the program can answer at different positions throughout 3D space. Density here controls visibility, not the cabinet’s weight. The original project explains this representation. One query 3D position + viewing direction → Neural network Uses its current weights → Two answers Color + density The network begins with untrained weights. During training, the photographs provide target pixel colors, while the renderer supplies the position-and-direction queries.

title: How the renderer generates 3D positions and viewing directions from a pixel
text: 2.6.4 Generate the 3D positions from a camera pixel In this example, COLMAP provides the estimated camera position, orientation, and lens parameters , as described in Section 2.6.2: Prepare images and camera parameters . NeRF’s renderer uses these outputs to calculate the sample positions and viewing directions: It selects a pixel in one training photograph. It uses COLMAP’s estimates of the camera position, orientation, and lens parameters to calculate the pixel’s ray : a line of sight extending into the scene. It samples several distances along that ray. Each distance gives a 3D sample position. It sends each position and the ray’s direction to the network. Points on the same ray share the same direction. P1–P3 are sample locations along the ray. The network is queried at these locations before any surface has been identified there. A small coordinate example Here, X points right, Y points toward the cabinet, and Z points up. Coordinates are in meters. The camera is at (0, −3, 0.64) . The selected ray points straight along +Y, so its direction is (0, 1, 0) . Sample Distance from camera 3D position sent to the network P1 1 m (0, −2, 0.64) P2 2 m (0, −1, 0.64) P3 2.54 m (0, −0.46, 0.64) For P2, start at the camera and move 2 m along +Y: the Y coordinate changes from −3 to −1. X and Z stay the same. Other pixels generally produce rays pointing in different directions. In practice, the renderer uses many samples, not just these three. Each sampled 3D position, together with the ray’s viewing direction, forms an input to the NeRF neural network. For P2, the input is position (0, −1, 0.64) and direction (0, 1, 0) . The network predicts a color and density for each sample. Section 2.6.5 explains how the renderer combines these predictions along the ray to produce one pixel’s color.

title: How NeRF renders cabinet samples into one pixel and then an image
text: 2.6.5 From network outputs to the selected pixel Section 2.6.4 calculated P1, P2, and P3 along the ray for one selected image pixel. Each position and the shared viewing direction are supplied as input to the same NeRF network. The network uses its current weights to calculate a color and density for each sample as output . For example, a prediction at P3, near the blue drawer front, could be: P3 input Position: (0, −0.46, 0.64) Direction: (0, 1, 0) → NeRF network Evaluates this input → P3 output Color: blue Density: high These outputs describe individual samples. The renderer still needs to combine them into one color for the original selected pixel . The diagram continues with the same camera, ray, and sample positions: P1–P3 keep the positions defined in Section 2.6.4. The marked pixel on the right is the pixel whose ray supplied those positions. A prediction that represents this cabinet well assigns low density to the air and blue color with high density near the drawer front: P1 · air Low density gives this sample little influence on the pixel’s color. P2 · air Low density again: most of the view continues toward the drawer. P3 · drawer Blue color and high density: samples around the front panel supply most of the pixel’s color and reduce the contribution from farther behind. The renderer combines the sample colors from near to far. Density and the distance represented by each sample determine how strongly it contributes and how much of the view passes through to later samples. This calculation is called volume rendering . It uses many samples along the ray; P1–P3 are three labeled locations within that process. Rendering details in the paper. The combined color is written into the original selected pixel. In this example, the drawer front makes that pixel blue. From one pixel to a complete cabinet image The renderer repeats the same calculation for every pixel, using a different ray for each one. The result is an ordinary 2D color image , like this cabinet view: Complete rendered view from the same camera. One ray gives one pixel. The ray through P1–P3 gives the blue pixel discussed above. All the rays give the whole picture. Rays through the drawer produce blue pixels; rays through the door produce gold pixels; rays through the body produce teal pixels. Rays that pass through empty space leave the white background visible. Color and density work together. Color supplies the possible colors along a ray. Density helps determine how much each sample contributes and how much is hidden behind it. After combining them, the finished pixel contains a single color. The prediction can still be wrong. Section 2.6.6 compares the rendered pixels with the corresponding photograph pixels and uses their differences to update the network.

title: The complete NeRF training loop: compare cabinet images and update weights
text: 2.6.6 Compare with the photograph, then learn In this example, the predicted drawer is gray, but the reference image shows blue. Both images use the same camera, so corresponding pixel colors can be compared directly. Current prediction The drawer color and edges are wrong. Photograph to match The reference drawer is blue. Render a prediction. Generate rays, query the network, and combine its answers. Measure the error. Compare the predicted colors with the corresponding photo pixels. Adjust the network’s weights. The training algorithm calculates changes intended to reduce that error. Repeat with more pixels and views. Render again with the updated network and compare again. The photographs provide target pixel colors, without labeling the density at P3 or the drawer’s surface position. Views from other cameras help constrain the 3D arrangement: a misplaced panel might match one view but appear in the wrong place in another. Rendering and comparison are repeated throughout training. As the network’s weights change to reduce image errors, its 3D description improves. One network is trained to account for the cabinet across the input views. The original training procedure.

title: Save the trained NeRF and render another view of the same cabinet
text: 2.6.7 Save the trained NeRF and render another view Training produces a NeRF network that represents this cabinet. Its learned weights are saved so the same network can be used again. The images rendered during training help check and improve that network, as described in Section 2.6.6 . Stage Input Result Train the NeRF Cabinet photographs + their camera parameters A trained network representing the cabinet in 3D Render a view The trained network + a chosen virtual camera A 2D image of the same cabinet from that camera To view the cabinet from farther to the right, move the virtual camera to the right. Keep the trained network unchanged. The renderer calculates new rays, queries the same network for color and density, and combines those outputs into a new image using the process in Section 2.6.5 . Rendering a viewpoint absent from the training photographs is called novel-view synthesis. This is a main use of NeRF: showing the same scene from another viewpoint. Each view is rendered directly from the trained network; the previously rendered image is not an input to this step. NeRF project and examples. Inspect the 3D answers Samples on several slices reveal the panels. These dots visualize answers; they are not what a NeRF stores. Same cabinet, another viewpoint The camera moves; the saved 3D representation stays the same. An unseen back or interior can still be wrong. Good-looking views do not guarantee accurate hidden geometry, moving joints, or mass. The stored scene differs from 3DGS : 3DGS adjusts a set of blobs; NeRF adjusts a network. Both use rendered images to check a 3D representation against photographs.

title: 2.7 Generate an asset with a pretrained model
text: 2.7 Generate an asset with a pretrained model Specific method · TRELLIS So far, we have adjusted one cabinet’s representation to match its photographs. A pretrained generator has already learned from many objects and uses that knowledge to propose a new 3D asset from an image or prompt. An asset is the object’s digital model.

title: From one image to a proposed 3D asset
text: 2.7.1 From one image to a proposed 3D asset Suppose only one photograph shows the cabinet’s front. It provides little direct evidence about the back or interior. A generator can use patterns learned during training to propose those unseen regions. The result is a plausible asset; hidden details still need inspection if we want to reproduce a particular real cabinet. TRELLIS is an example of a 3D asset generator. Give its image-based model a cabinet picture, and it can create a 3D result using its prior training. It can output that result as a mesh, 3D Gaussians, or a radiance field. TRELLIS project. The method and its output are different things: TRELLIS is the system that creates the asset; mesh, Gaussians, and radiance field describe ways to represent its result. These are the representations introduced in Section 2.1 . Mesh output Vertices and connected faces describe surfaces. Appearance can be supplied with textures and materials. Gaussian output Positions, shapes, opacity, and appearance describe blobs that a Gaussian renderer blends into views. Radiance field output Color and density describe the scene at locations in 3D. To make a picture, provide the field and a virtual camera to a compatible volume renderer . It reads color and density along camera rays and combines them into pixels, as in Section 2.6.5 . For the cabinet, choose a camera on its right to render a right-side view. Keep the field unchanged; choose another camera to make another view. The next tool depends on the output: a mesh editor or mesh renderer for meshes, a Gaussian viewer or renderer for Gaussians, and a compatible volume renderer for radiance fields. TRELLIS provides a renderer for its own radiance-field output. Its official example uses it to make a video from a sequence of camera views. The field’s saved form can differ from the original NeRF network described in Section 2.6.

title: Compare the representations
text: 2.7.2 Compare the representations A generator can save a 3D result in different forms. The cabinet below illustrates what those forms look like: a mesh stores connected surfaces, while Gaussians store colored blobs in 3D. One cabinet picture A front view is a flat image. It does not show the cabinet’s hidden sides. Mesh representation Connected surfaces describe the shape. Lines reveal the triangular faces. Gaussian representation Projecting and blending the 3D blobs makes this picture. These are scripted teaching views of a constructed cabinet, not TRELLIS predictions. See the TRELLIS gallery for the authors’ model results. Both representations can show color. The mesh and Gaussian views here share a camera and color scheme. The triangle lines help us inspect the mesh; a renderer can hide those lines and use textures and materials to show its appearance. Why would we choose a mesh? Suppose we want a robot to grasp the cabinet handle. We need to locate the handle’s surface and the gap behind it, edit the shape if necessary, and prepare shapes for contact. A mesh gives us explicit surface patches to work with. We can also organize its geometry into parts before adding joints and physical properties. If our immediate goal is to reproduce the look of a photographed scene from new viewpoints, 3DGS is designed for that rendering task. Its colored blobs can capture appearance without first building a connected surface. The choice depends on what we want to do with the result; surface geometry and Gaussian appearance can also be used together. Original 3DGS project .

title: Conclusion: create, store, then render
text: 2.7.3 Conclusion: create, store, then render Input image A cabinet photograph. Generate TRELLIS proposes a 3D asset using its prior training. Keep a supported representation For example, a mesh, Gaussians, or a radiance field. Render The appropriate renderer makes a view from a chosen camera. The Gaussian rendering operation can draw Gaussians produced by a generator as well as Gaussians fitted to photographs. The renderer uses the stored parameters; how those parameters were obtained is a separate part of the workflow. In the original 3DGS and NeRF examples, photographs of one cabinet guide scene-specific fitting. With a system such as TRELLIS, a pretrained generator proposes an asset from an image. Both routes produce 3D information that can be rendered and inspected.

title: 3.1 What is an articulated object?
text: 3.1 What is an articulated object? An articulated object is made of parts that can move relative to one another. A drawer slides. A door swings. The cabinet holds them together. The cabinet below has two independent movements: the drawer slides and the door rotates. Its connections determine which movements are possible. Watch the cabinet animation. Body Stays fixed in this example. Drawer Slides in and out along a straight line. Door Rotates around its hinge.

title: Links and joints
text: 3.1.1 Links and joints We describe this cabinet using two building blocks: links and joints . Link A rigid part: its shape stays the same as it moves. The body, drawer, and door are three links. Joint A connection that defines how two links can move relative to each other. The door’s hinge connects the door to the body and lets it rotate. A handle fixed to the door moves together with the door, so it can be included in the same link. A handle that turns independently needs its own link and joint.

title: How joints let parts move
text: 3.1.2 How joints let parts move The drawer and door move in different ways. Move the sliders to try each joint. Sliding Prismatic joint Drawer opening 20 cm 0 cm 50 cm The direction stays the same. Only the distance changes. Rotating Revolute joint Door opening 35° 0° 90° The hinge stays in place. Only the angle changes. The allowed range is the joint’s motion limit . Here, the drawer opens from 0 to 50 cm, and the door from 0° to 90°. These are illustrative limits; another cabinet may allow different motion.

title: Degrees of freedom
text: 3.1.3 Degrees of freedom One articulated object can have several degrees of freedom. This cabinet is one object, but it has two movable joints: one for the drawer and one for the door. A degree of freedom (DOF) is an independent motion you can control. With the cabinet body held fixed: Part Independent control DOF Drawer How far it slides 1 Door How far it rotates 1 Whole cabinet Drawer and door move independently 2 You can leave the door still and move the drawer. You can also leave the drawer still and move the door. So describing the whole cabinet’s pose takes two numbers : the drawer’s opening distance and the door’s opening angle. Here, each joint has 1 DOF; the whole cabinet has 2 DOF. Opening the drawer farther changes its position, but it still has the same one degree of freedom.

title: Kinematic trees
text: 3.1.4 Kinematic trees A kinematic tree records which parts are connected. Each node is a link; each connecting line is a joint. The body is the root : the starting link of this tree. It is the parent of the drawer and door; they are its children . The tree describes connections, not the parts’ positions on the page. In the example below, we add a turning latch to the drawer. The latch can turn independently, adding one more degree of freedom: this version has 3 DOF . Select a part in the tree, then play its motion. The object Its connections hinge slide turn Body Door Drawer Latch Drawer. Slides relative to the body. The latch comes along because it is attached to the drawer. Play drawer motion Motion position Reset A moving part carries its children The drawer is the latch’s parent in this tree. When the drawer slides, the latch travels with it. The latch can also turn relative to the drawer. The door is on a different branch, so moving the drawer does not move the door. Not every articulated object forms a tree. Some mechanisms contain closed loops. This example focuses on a tree, where each link other than the root has one parent.
